strengths: The paper offers an original, useful simplification of difficult three-view pose estimation: generate approximate virtual correspondences and reuse established 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers. The training-free mean-point construction is especially appealing for practical adoption. This supported contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance despite the reservations below.

The real-data results establish competitiveness with dedicated four-point methods. Across 10,000 PhotoTourism triplets, Table 1 shows that the mean-plus-shift solver improves Sacre Coeur AUC@10 from 50.61 for the homotopy baseline to 52.27. On KITTI, Table 2 reports comparable pose accuracy to 6pt+P3P while reducing average RANSAC runtime from 0.11 to 0.07 seconds.

The experiments include meaningful controls: larger-sample baselines, homotopy continuation, oracle correspondences, controlled noise and outliers, and shift ablations. Figure 3 supports improved convergence per RANSAC iteration under substantial outlier contamination. The synthetic and real correspondence experiments, together with the supplementary geometric lemma, provide useful support for the centroid heuristic.

The manuscript acknowledges that its solvers are approximate and that 5pt+P3P remains preferable in some settings. The distinction between sampling configurations is valuable, and the supplementary architecture and training details make the learned component easier to assess.
weaknesses: The claimed advantage under limited computation is only partially established. The outlier plots compare RANSAC iterations, although iteration costs differ substantially: Table 1 reports 218.71 microseconds for the mean-plus-shift solver versus 77.90 for 5pt+P3P, with learned variants costing 450–1130 microseconds. Accuracy versus elapsed time is needed to establish the claimed benefit at equal computational budgets. The learned variants also deliver modest improvements for their additional cost.

Validation of the unknown-focal contribution is incomplete. The real-data evaluation uses KITTI stereo pairs plus an adjacent temporal view and reports pose errors without focal-length errors. Moreover, the three-view metric evaluates rotation and translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, leaving the relative baseline scale unmeasured. Consequently, the experiments do not fully assess the claimed joint camera-geometry recovery.

The approximation has a substantial noiseless error floor in Figure 6. The supplementary lemma bounds an image-space residual by triangle size, which does not guarantee accurate pose recovery under poor conditioning. With the principal calibrated evaluation concentrated on two landmark scenes, performance under strong perspective distortion, large depth variation, and small baselines remains insufficiently characterized. These limitations constrain applicability rather than negate the demonstrated RANSAC utility.

Equation (2) defines a signed normalized epipolar residual as the training loss. Minimizing that expression does not necessarily move a prediction toward the epipolar line; a nonnegative loss and precise Sampson normalization are required. This may be a notation error, but the manuscript does not resolve the discrepancy. It affects reproducibility of the learned variant, while the mean-point construction is independent of it.

Experimental reproduction remains underspecified: RANSAC thresholds, stopping settings, local refinement, and handling of multiple solver hypotheses are not described sufficiently. Source code is promised rather than supplied in the manuscript. These are correctable reporting gaps, but they matter when the measured accuracy and runtime depend strongly on the surrounding robust-estimation implementation.
